reasoning.Student A:
My goal is to maximize my chances of getting my most preferred school. Since my outcome is determined by my priorities at each school and my own preferences, I need to consider my priority rank at each school.

I have priority 1 at both y and w. I have priority 2 at both x and z.

Since y is my most preferred school and I have top priority there, I should rank it first. This guarantees I get y if it's obtainable, and since I have priority 1 it is very likely to be obtainable.

Next, I prefer z to w and x. I have priority 2 at z. I prefer w to x, and I have priority 1 at w. Therefore, I should rank w second. This is because if I don't get y, I have a good chance to get w, where I have top priority.

Finally, I need to decide between z and x. I prefer z to x, and I have priority 2 at both. Therefore, I should rank z before x.

Therefore, my ranking should be: y > w > z > x.
reasoning.Student B:
My goal is to be matched to the best school possible according to my preferences: z > y > w > x. My outcome is determined by the intersection of my preferences and the schools I can get into (my "obtainable set").

School z: I have priority 1 at z. This means z is definitely in my obtainable set.

School y: I have priority 2 at y. It's possible y is in my obtainable set, but it depends on how many other students apply to y and have higher priority than me.

School w: I have priority 2 at w. It's possible w is in my obtainable set, but it depends on how many other students apply to w and have higher priority than me.

School x: I have priority 1 at x. This means x is definitely in my obtainable set.

Since z is my most preferred school and I have the highest priority at z, I should rank z first. Since x is my least preferred school but I have the highest priority at x, I should rank x last. This is because if I don't include x at all, and I am rejected from z, y, and w, then I will be unmatched.

Now I need to decide the order of y and w. I prefer y > w. Since I have the same priority at both schools, I should rank y before w.

Therefore, my ranking should be z > y > w > x.
reasoning.Student C:
My goal is to be matched to the school I most prefer from the set of schools that would accept me. My preferences are z > y > w > x. The order I rank the schools only affects which school I get from the set of schools that would accept me.

I should rank the schools in order of my preference: z > y > w > x. This is because if z is obtainable, I want to be matched to z. If z is not obtainable, but y is, I want to be matched to y, and so on. Ranking in any other order would mean I might get a less preferred school even if a more preferred school was obtainable.
